claims.source: We found that Activin A treatment increased the expression of Atoh1 and the Wnt-target gene Lgr5 by more than 4-fold
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Activin A treatment increases the expression of Lgr5 by more than 4-fold.
claims.source: We found that Activin A treatment increased the expression of Atoh1 and the Wnt-target gene Lgr5 by more than 4-fold
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Activin A treatment increases the expression of Pou4f3 by more than 12-fold.
claims.source: and increased the expression of Pou4f3, a critical early hair cell-specific transcription factor by more than 12-fold.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Activin treatment leads to a more than 2-fold reduction in Bmp4, Id2, Id3 and Id4 expression.
claims.source: Furthermore, Activin treatment led to a more than 2-fold reduction in Bmp4, Id2, Id3 and Id4 expression
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Activin treatment does not significantly alter the expression of p27/Kip1, Etv5, Hey1, Hey2, Fgf20 and Ptch1.
claims.source: but did not significantly alter the expression of other pro-sensory genes (p27/Kip1- official gene name Cdkn1b, Etv5, Hey1, Hey2, Fgf20 and Ptch1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: BMP receptor signaling positively regulates Id1-3 expression in cochlear and vestibular pro-sensory cells.
claims.source: BMP receptor signaling has been shown to positively regulate Id1-3 expression in cochlear and vestibular pro-sensory cells (Kamaid et al., 2010; Ohyama et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Brief BMP4 treatment significantly increases Id1 and Id3 expression but has no effect on Id4 and Atoh1 expression.
claims.source: Brief BMP4 treatment significantly increased Id1 and Id3 expression compared to control but had no effect on Id4 and Atoh1 expression (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Brief Activin A treatment results in a modest but significant decrease in Id4 expression but does not alter Id1-3 or Atoh1 expression.
claims.source: Conversely, the brief Activin A treatment resulted in a modest, but significant decrease in Id4 expression compared to control but did not alter Id1-3 or Atoh1 expression (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Activin A selectively stimulates the phosphorylation of SMAD2/3 in the developing cochlea.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that in the developing cochlea Activin A selectively stimulated the phosphorylation of SMAD2/3, whereas BMP4 treatment selectively induced the phosphorylation of SMAD1/5/9 (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: BMP4 treatment selectively induces the phosphorylation of SMAD1/5/9 in the developing cochlea.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that in the developing cochlea Activin A selectively stimulated the phosphorylation of SMAD2/3, whereas BMP4 treatment selectively induced the phosphorylation of SMAD1/5/9 (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Activin A positively regulates Atoh1 expression through an indirect mechanism that involves the repression of BMP-dependent and independent Id gene expression.
claims.source: Taken together these findings suggests that Activin A positively regulates Atoh1 expression through an indirect mechanism that, at least in part, involves the repression of BMP-dependent and independent Id gene expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing differential effects of Activin A on Id gene expression.

claims.claim: FST overexpressing cochlear tissue lacks hair cells at E14.5 while control cochlear tissue already contains inner hair cells at the base of the cochlea.
claims.source: While control cochlear tissue already contained inner hair cells at the base of the cochlea, as shown here using cochlear whole mounts and sections, FST overexpressing cochlear tissue still lacked hair cells (Figure 3C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FST overexpression experiments shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claims.claim: Atoh1 and Pou4f3 mRNA expression is significantly reduced in E14.5 FST overexpressing cochlear epithelia.
claims.source: Consistent with FST antagonizing hair cell differentiation, we found that Atoh1 and Pou4f3 mRNA expression was significantly reduced in E14.5 FST overexpressing cochlear epithelia
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Id3 and Id4 mRNA expression is significantly increased in E14.5 FST overexpressing cochlear epithelia compared to control.
claims.source: whereas the mRNA expression of Id3 and Id4 was significantly increased compared to control (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: FST overexpression results in a modest but significant increase in the expression of Ptch1 and Etv5.
claims.source: In addition, FST overexpression resulted in a modest but significant increase in the expression of the SHH receptor encoding gene Ptch1 (Driver et al., 2008) and the FGFR target and effector gene Etv5 (Hayashi et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The expression of Fgf20, Hey1 and Hey2 remains unchanged in response to FST overexpression.
claims.source: Despite these changes, the expression of Fgf20, Hey1 and Hey2, which are targets and effectors of SHH/FGFR signaling (Benito-Gonzalez and Doetzlhofer, 2014; Tateya et al., 2013), remained unchanged in response to FST overexpression (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: FST overexpression leads to a modest but significant reduction in the expression of Bmp4.
claims.source: Interestingly, FST overexpression also led to a modest but significant reduction in the expression of Bmp4.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: FST overexpression significantly reduces P-SMAD2/3 protein levels in the developing cochlea.
claims.source: Consistent with its role as a canonical Activin antagonist, overexpression of FST significantly reduced P-SMAD2/3 protein levels in the developing cochlea.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claims.claim: Cochlear P-SMAD1/5/9 protein levels remain unchanged in response to FST overexpression.
claims.source: By contrast, cochlear P-SMAD1/5/9 protein levels, a readout for BMP signaling, remained unchanged in response to FST overexpression (Figure 3F,G)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claims.claim: FST overexpression does not disrupt BMP signaling in the developing cochlea.
claims.source: suggesting that FST overexpression does not disrupt BMP signaling in the developing cochlea.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Western blot data showing unchanged P-SMAD1/5/9 levels.

claims.claim: Hair cell differentiation occurs significantly earlier in Activin A-treated wild type cochlear explants compared to untreated wild type cochlear explants.
claims.source: Consistent with our earlier findings, we observed that hair cell differentiation occurred significantly earlier in Activin A-treated wild type cochlear explants compared to untreated wild type cochlear explants (Figure 4B,C,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures shown in Figures 4B, 4C, and 4F.

claims.claim: The onset of hair cell differentiation is significantly delayed in untreated FST overexpressing cochlear explants compared to untreated wild type cochlear explants.
claims.source: Conversely, the onset of hair cell differentiation was significantly delayed in untreated FST overexpressing cochlear explants compared to untreated wild type cochlear explants (Figure 4B,D,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures shown in Figures 4B, 4D, and 4F.

claims.claim: Activin A treatment rescues the FST-mediated delay in hair cell differentiation.
claims.source: These defects were almost completely abolished when Activin A treatment and FST overexpression were combined and no significant differences in the onset or in the progression of hair cell differentiation was observed between FST overexpressing cochlear explants treated with Activin A and wild type untreated cochlear explants (Figure 4B,E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures shown in Figures 4B, 4E, and 4F.

claims.claim: FST antagonizes hair cell differentiation in an Activin A-dependent manner.
claims.source: In summary, our data suggest that FST antagonizes hair cell differentiation in an Activin A-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the rescue experiments showing that Activin A can overcome FST-mediated delays.

claims.claim: Induction of FST overexpression at E11.5 or E14.5 results in neonatal lethality of R26-FST transgenic animals.
claims.source: Induction of FST overexpression at E11.5 or as late as E14.5 resulted in neonatal lethality of R26-FST transgenic animals, limiting our analysis to late embryonic stages.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedures.

claims.claim: R26-FST cochlear tissue contains two rows of inner hair cells throughout the basal half of the cochlea at E18.5.
claims.source: By contrast, R26-FST cochlear tissue contained two rows of inner hair cells throughout the basal half of the cochlea (Figure 5A,B, R26-FST).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: The density of inner phalangeal cells is similarly increased in response to FST overexpression.
claims.source: The observed ectopic inner hair cells were unlikely to be the product of supporting cell-to-hair cell fate conversion, as the density of supporting cells that surrounded inner hair cells-called inner phalangeal cells- was similarly increased in response to FST overexpression (Figure 5C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: The outer hair cell density and cellular patterning is unchanged in response to FST overexpression except for the cochlear base.
claims.source: Interestingly, the outer hair cell density and cellular patterning was unchanged in response to FST overexpression except for the cochlear base.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: The base of FST overexpressing cochleae contains short stretches of sensory epithelium in which the third row of outer hair cells is missing.
claims.source: The base of FST overexpressing cochleae contained short stretches of sensory epithelium in which the third row of outer hair cells was missing, resulting in a modest reduction in outer hair cell density (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: Differentiation/maturation of the auditory sensory epithelium is severely delayed in response to FST overexpression.
claims.source: Furthermore, differentiation/maturation of the auditory sensory epithelium was severely delayed in response to FST overexpression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple observations including delayed stereocilia formation and reduced cochlear length.

claims.claim: Auditory sensory epithelia from R26-FST transgenic animals are 30% shorter compared to auditory sensory epithelia from control littermates at E18.5.
claims.source: Consistent with a severe delay in hair cell differentiation, auditory sensory epithelia from R26-FST transgenic animals had not yet thinned to a single layer of supporting cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and their length was 30% shorter compared to auditory sensory epithelia from control littermates (single transgenic control = 5.14 ± 0.04 mm, R26-FST = 3.65 ± 0.13 mm, n = 5, p=0.0002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Hair cells in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue have less mature stereocilia than their wild type counterparts at E18.5.
claims.source: Moreover, hair cells in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue had less mature stereocilia than their wild type counterparts, and apical hair cells lacked stereocilia completely (Figure 5B, R26-FST).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: FST induction at E13.0 has no effect on the length of the auditory sensory epithelium at E17.5.
claims.source: FST induction one day later at ~E13.0 (dox E12.5), had no effect on the length of the auditory sensory epithelium (dox E12.5, harvest E17.5: single transgenic control = 4.13 ± 0.17 mm, R26-FST = 3.99 ± 0.12 mm, n = 3, p=0.5425).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Ectopic inner hair cells continue to be observed when FST is induced at E13.0, with the highest number found in the basal portion of the auditory sensory epithelium.
claims.source: However, we continued to observe ectopic inner hair cells in FST overexpressing cochleae, with the highest number of ectopic hair cells found in the basal portion of the auditory sensory epithelium, as well as short stretches of sensory epithelium with only two rows of outer hair cells (Figure 6A,B)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claims.claim: FST induction as late as E13.0 causes a delay in hair cell differentiation/maturation.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that hair cell stereocilia in FST overexpressing cochleae had a less mature phenotype compared to their counterparts in control cochlear tissue, indicating that FST induction as late as ~E13.0 causes a delay in hair cells differentiation/maturation (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The conditional knockout of the Inhba gene does not alter overall cochlear morphology or the length of the sensory epithelium at P0.
claims.source: The conditional knockout (cKO) of the Inhba gene did not alter overall cochlear morphology, nor did it alter the length of the sensory epithelium compared to control (Inhba fl/fl) (P0: control = 4.99 ± 0.12 mm; Inhba cKO = 4. 82 ± 0.01 mm; n = 2, p-value=0.4043).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Loss of Inhba gene function results in hair cell maturation and patterning defects.
claims.source: However, as predicted, loss of Inhba gene function resulted in hair cell maturation and patterning defects.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Inhba conditional knockout mice.

claims.claim: Inhba cKO cochlear tissue shows a significant increase in the number of ectopic inner hair cells compared to control.
claims.source: By contrast, Inhba cKO cochlear tissue showed a significant increase in the number of ectopic inner hair cells compared to control, with more of the ectopic inner hair cells residing within the most basal segment (Figure 6C, Inhba cKO, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: Hair cell stereocilia in Inhba mutant cochlear tissue have a less mature phenotype compared to their counterparts in control cochlear tissue.
claims.source: Furthermore, consistent with a delayed onset of hair cell differentiation, hair cell stereocilia in the base, mid and apex of Inhba mutant cochlear tissue had a less mature phenotype compared to their counterparts in control cochlear tissue (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Inhba (Activin A) function is required for limiting inner hair cell formation and for timing hair cell differentiation/maturation in vivo.
claims.source: Taken together, our findings demonstrate that Inhba (Activin A) function is required for limiting inner hair cell formation as well as for timing hair cell differentiation/maturation in vivo.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data from Inhba conditional knockout mice.

claims.claim: FST likely disrupts other Activin-related signaling mechanisms in addition to Activin A signaling in the developing cochlea.
claims.source: The milder defects in cochlear hair cell formation observed in Inhba mutants suggest that in addition to Activin A signaling, FST likely disrupts other, Activin-related signaling mechanisms in the developing cochlea.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing the phenotypes of FST overexpression and Inhba deletion.

claims.claim: Activin B (Inhbb), GDF11 and Myostatin (Mstn) activate SMAD2/3 signaling and are high affinity binding partners of FST.
claims.source: Like Activin A, Activin B (Inhbb) and the Activin-related ligands GDF11 and Myostatin (Mstn) activate SMAD2/3 signaling and are high affinity binding partners of FST (Thompson et al., 2005; Walker et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Gdf11 transcript is abundantly expressed at the onset of and during cochlear differentiation.
claims.source: We found Gdf11 transcript to be abundantly expressed at the onset of (E13.5) as well as during (E14.5, E15.5) cochlear differentiation, making it a likely candidate for FST-mediated regulation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Inhbb and Mstn transcripts are undetectable or expressed at very low levels in the developing cochlear epithelial duct.
claims.source: By contrast, Inhbb and Mstn transcripts were undetectable or expressed at very low levels.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In the murine cochlea, cell cycle exit occurs within a 48 hr time window, with apically located pro-sensory cells exiting as early as E12.5 and basal pro-sensory cells exiting as late as E14.5.
claims.source: In the murine cochlea, cell cycle exit occurs within a 48 hr time window, with apically located pro-sensory cells exiting the cell cycle as early as E12.5 and pro-sensory cells located in the base of the cochlea exiting as late as E14.5 (Lee et al., 2006; Ruben, 1967).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Hair cells located in the basal turn of the cochlea incorporate EdU at high rate (~25%) in both control and R26-FST transgenic animals when EdU is administered at E13.5.
claims.source: Consistent with previous reports, we found that hair cells located in the basal turn of the cochlea incorporated EdU at high rate (~25%) in both control and R26-FST transgenic animals (Figure 7A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figures 7A-C.

claims.claim: Control cochlear hair cells located in the mid and apex show little to no EdU incorporation when EdU is administered at E13.5, while their counterparts in FST overexpressing cochleae exhibit robust EdU incorporation.
claims.source: However, while control cochlear hair cells located further apically (mid and apex) showed little to no EdU incorporation, their counterparts in FST overexpressing cochleae exhibited robust EdU incorporation (Figure 7A–C)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figures 7A-C.

claims.claim: FST overexpression in the developing cochlea delays pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal.
claims.source: indicating that FST overexpression in the developing cochlea delays pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EdU incorporation data.

claims.claim: FST overexpression does not disrupt the apical-to-basal gradient of pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal.
claims.source: FST overexpression did not disrupt the apical-to-basal gradient of pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EdU incorporation data showing that apical hair cells still incorporate EdU at lower rates than basal hair cells in FST overexpressing tissue.

claims.claim: In wild type cochlear tissue, inner hair cell progenitors withdraw from the cell cycle prior to outer hair cell progenitor cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, our analysis revealed that in wild type cochlear tissue inner and outer hair cell progenitors did not withdraw from the cell cycle at the same time. We found that in the mid-turn of control cochleae more than 6% of outer hair cells were labeled with EdU, whereas no EdU incorporation was found in inner hair cells, suggesting that inner hair cell progenitors had exited the cell cycle prior to the more laterally located outer hair cell progenitors (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: No difference in the frequency of EdU incorporation among inner and outer hair cells is observed in FST overexpressing cochleae.
claims.source: By contrast, no difference in the frequency of EdU incorporation among inner and outer hair cells was observed in FST overexpressing cochleae (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Supporting cells and hair cells in R26-FST transgenic animals incorporate EdU at much higher frequency than their counterparts in control animals when EdU is administered daily from E14.5 to E17.5.
claims.source: Again, consistent with a severe delay in pro-sensory cell cycle exit, supporting cells and hair cells in R26-FST transgenic animals incorporated EdU at much higher frequency than their counterparts in control (single transgenic) animals (Figure 8A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figures 8A-D.

claims.claim: In control cochlear tissue, the percentage of outer hair cells that incorporated EdU (12.1%) is significantly higher compared to the percentage of inner hair cells that incorporated EdU (1.5%).
claims.source: In control cochlear tissue, consistent with the existence of a medial-to-lateral gradient of cell cycle withdrawal, the percentage of outer hair cells (12.1%) that incorporated EdU was significantly higher compared to the percentage of inner hair cells (1.5%) that incorporated EdU (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: In FST overexpressing cochlear tissue, inner hair cells incorporate EdU at a similar or higher rate than outer hair cells.
claims.source: By contrast, in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue, inner hair cells incorporated EdU at a similar or higher rate than outer hair cells (Figure 8F)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 8F.

claims.claim: In the apex of FST overexpressing cochlear tissue, inner hair cells and their surrounding inner phalangeal cells are the only cell types labeled with EdU.
claims.source: and in its apex inner hair cells and their surrounding inner phalangeal cells were the only cell types that were labeled with EdU (Figure 8A,B,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figures 8A, 8B, and 8D.

claims.claim: The ectopic hair cells observed in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue are, at least in part, the product of prolonged proliferation of inner hair cell progenitor cells.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the ectopic hair cells observed in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue are, at least in part, the product of prolonged proliferation of inner hair cell progenitor cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EdU incorporation data showing prolonged proliferation of inner hair cell progenitors.

claims.claim: Activin A acts as a pro-differentiation signal in the mammalian cochlea.
claims.source: We find that exogenous Activin A triggers premature hair cell differentiation in cochlear explant cultures and demonstrate that disruption of Activin A signaling due to FST overexpression or Inhba deletion results in a delay in cochlear hair cell differentiation in vivo.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures and genetic manipulations.

claims.claim: Activin signaling promotes cortical interneuron differentiation through the inhibition of SHH signaling.
claims.source: For instance, Activin signaling has been shown to promote cortical interneuron differentiation, at least in part, through the inhibition of SHH signaling (Cambray et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Neither over-activation nor loss of Activin signaling alters the expression of SHH target and effector genes Hey1, Hey2 and Fgf20.
claims.source: However, we found no evidence for direct interference as neither over-activation nor loss of Activin signaling altered the expression of SHH target and effector genes Hey1, Hey2 and Fgf20 (Benito-Gonzalez and Doetzlhofer, 2014; Tateya et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Activin signaling does not activate Atoh1 expression directly but rather through indirect mechanisms.
claims.source: However, a brief 4 hr Activin A treatment failed to significantly increase Atoh1 transcript abundance, suggesting that Activin signaling does not activate Atoh1 expression directly but rather through indirect mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing no immediate increase in Atoh1 expression after brief Activin A treatment.

claims.claim: Activin signaling positively regulates ATOH1 activity/expression through inhibiting cochlear expression of Id3 and Id4.
claims.source: Indeed, our findings suggest that Activin signaling positively regulates ATOH1 activity/expression through inhibiting cochlear expression of Id3 and Id4.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing reduced Id3 and Id4 expression in response to Activin A treatment.

claims.claim: A failure to downregulate Id3 expression in hair cell progenitors inhibits the formation of hair cells in both auditory and vestibular sensory organs.
claims.source: Consistent with an inhibitory role in hair cell differentiation, previous studies found that a failure to downregulate Id3 expression in hair cell progenitors inhibits the formation of hair cells in both auditory and vestibular sensory organs (Jones et al., 2006; Kamaid et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Atoh1 expression and subsequent hair cell differentiation is delayed but not disrupted in response to FST overexpression or Inhba ablation.
claims.source: It should be noted that Atoh1 expression and subsequent hair cell differentiation is not disrupted, but rather delayed in response to FST overexpression or Inhba ablation, suggesting the existence of Activin-independent mechanisms capable of activating Atoh1 expression in pro-sensory cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claims.claim: The Wnt effector β-catenin is required for hair cell specification and has been shown to directly activate Atoh1 transcription in neuronal progenitors.
claims.source: The Wnt effector β-catenin is required for hair cell specification and has been shown to directly activate Atoh1 transcription in neuronal progenitors (Shi et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling initiates Atoh1 expression, whereas Activin signaling functions to enhance Atoh1 expression/activity along the longitudinal cochlear axis.
claims.source: Taking these recent findings and our findings into consideration, we propose a model in which Wnt/β-catenin signaling initiates Atoh1 expression, whereas Activin signaling functions to enhance Atoh1 expression/activity along the longitudinal cochlear axis.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on inference from the current findings and previous studies.

claims.claim: Early SHH signaling from the ventral midline is critical for establishing regional identity in the developing cochlea, including the distinct basal–apical pattern of Inhba and Fst expression.
claims.source: Early SHH signaling, presumably from the ventral midline, is critical for establishing regional identity in the developing cochlea, including setting up the distinct basal–apical pattern of Inhba and Fst expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and inference.

claims.claim: Subsequent SHH signaling from the spiral ganglion is dispensable for establishing/maintaining Inhba and Fst expression.
claims.source: However, subsequent SHH signaling from the spiral ganglion is dispensable for establishing/maintaining Inhba and Fst expression (Son et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Notch signaling positively regulates Inhba expression in differentiating and terminal differentiated supporting cells.
claims.source: Notch signaling is active in pro-sensory cells and has been shown to positively regulate Inhba expression in differentiating and terminal differentiated supporting cells (Campbell et al., 2016; Maass et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: FST overexpression delays the onset of pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal and differentiation.
claims.source: We show that FST overexpression delays the onset of pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal and differentiation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from EdU incorporation experiments.

claims.claim: LIN28B plays a similar function to FST in timing pro-sensory cell withdrawal and differentiation.
claims.source: A similar function in timing pro-sensory cell withdrawal and differentiation has been recently reported for the RNA binding protein LIN28B (Golden et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The expression of Fst in the developing cochlea largely mimics that of Lin28b.
claims.source: Interestingly, the expression of Fst in the developing cochlea largely mimics that of Lin28b; each are initially highly expressed in pro-sensory cells and are downregulated upon differentiation following a basal-to-apical gradient.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of expression patterns from the current study and previous studies.

claims.claim: TGF-β-related signaling pathways inhibit proliferation through promoting the expression and/or activity of cyclin dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitors.
claims.source: TGF-β-related signaling pathways are known to inhibit proliferation through promoting the expression and/or activity of cyclin dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitors (Massagué and Gomis, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: The CDK inhibitor p27/Kip1 (CDKN1B) is the main regulator of pro-sensory cell cycle exit in the developing cochlea.
claims.source: In the developing cochlea, the CDK inhibitor p27/Kip1 (CDKN1B) is the main regulator of pro-sensory cell cycle exit and its transcriptional upregulation directs the apical-to-basal wave of pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal (Chen and Segil, 1999; Lee et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: No changes in p27/Kip1 mRNA expression are observed in response to FST overexpression.
claims.source: However, we observed no changes in p27/Kip1 mRNA expression in response to FST overexpression
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The observed delay in pro-sensory cell cycle exit may be due to a reduction in p27/Kip1 protein stability and/or activity.
claims.source: suggesting that the observed delay in pro-sensory cell cycle exit may instead be due to a reduction in p27/Kip1 protein stability and/or activity.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The increase in Id3 and Id4 expression in response to FST overexpression likely contributed to the observed delay in pro-sensory cell cycle exit.
claims.source: In addition, it is likely that the increase in Id3 and Id4 expression in response to FST overexpression contributed to the observed delay in pro-sensory cell cycle exit.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the experimental data and established knowledge about ID proteins.

claims.claim: High ID protein expression is associated with a proliferative, undifferentiated cell state.
claims.source: High ID protein expression is associated with a proliferative, undifferentiated cell state and ID4 expression in spermatogonia and mammary glands is a predictor for stemness (Helsel et al., 2017; Wang and Baker, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Fst can be detected within the most ventral aspect of the developing otocyst as early as E10.5, preceding Activin A expression by several days.
claims.source: This is quite likely as Fst can be detected within the most ventral aspect of the developing otocyst as early as E10.5, preceding Activin A expression by several days (Son et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The cochlear defects observed in Inhba mutants are much milder compared to the cochlear defects observed in FST transgenic animals.
claims.source: Furthermore, the cochlear defects observed in Inhba mutants are much milder compared to the cochlear defects observed in FST transgenic animals.

results.result: Inhba and Fst are expressed in opposing gradients within the developing cochlea that correlate with the spatial and temporal pattern of hair cell differentiation. At E13.5, Inhba expression is limited to the basal pro-sensory domain where Atoh1 expression begins, while Fst is highly expressed in the apex and mid-turn but weakly in the base. As differentiation progresses (E14.5-E15.5), Inhba expression extends apically while Fst expression regresses basally, creating a counter-gradient that parallels the basal-to-apical wave of hair cell differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 are well-supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 1A-C demonstrating the opposing expression gradients of Inhba and Fst across developmental stages. The spatial and temporal correlation between these gradients and Atoh1 expression provides strong evidence for the proposed relationship, though the inference in C34 about pro-sensory cells being exposed to an Activin A signaling gradient is reasonable but indirect.

results.result: Exogenous Activin A treatment promotes precocious hair cell differentiation in E13.5 cochlear explants. After 12 hours of Activin A treatment, GFP-positive inner hair cells are evident in treated explants but not controls, and the band of differentiated cells extends further apically at all time points examined. Activin A treatment increases expression of hair cell markers (Atoh1 >4-fold, Lgr5 >4-fold, Pou4f3 >12-fold) and decreases expression of differentiation inhibitors (Bmp4, Id2, Id3, Id4 >2-fold reduction) without affecting other pro-sensory genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C43 are strongly supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures (Figure 2B-D) showing both morphological evidence of precocious differentiation and quantitative RT-qPCR data demonstrating specific transcriptional changes. The consistency between the morphological observations and molecular changes provides converging evidence for Activin A's pro-differentiation role.

results.result: Activin A and BMP4 have distinct effects on Id gene expression and activate different SMAD pathways in the developing cochlea. Brief BMP4 treatment increases Id1 and Id3 expression but not Id4 or Atoh1, while brief Activin A treatment modestly decreases Id4 expression without affecting Id1-3 or Atoh1. Activin A selectively stimulates SMAD2/3 phosphorylation while BMP4 selectively induces SMAD1/5/9 phosphorylation, suggesting Activin A regulates Atoh1 indirectly through repression of Id gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 2F) and Western blot analysis (Figure 2G) demonstrating differential responses to Activin A versus BMP4 treatment. The selective SMAD phosphorylation patterns confirm distinct signaling pathways. However, the mechanistic inference in C49 about indirect regulation is reasonable but not definitively proven by these data alone.

results.result: FST overexpression delays hair cell differentiation and antagonizes Activin signaling in the developing cochlea. At E14.5, FST overexpressing cochlear tissue lacks hair cells present in controls, shows reduced Atoh1 and Pou4f3 expression, and increased Id3 and Id4 expression. FST overexpression significantly reduces P-SMAD2/3 protein levels (indicating reduced Activin signaling) but does not affect P-SMAD1/5/9 levels (indicating intact BMP signaling).
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C58 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including morphological analysis (Figures 3C-D), RT-qPCR data (Figure 3E), and Western blot analysis (Figures 3F-G). The selective reduction in P-SMAD2/3 without affecting P-SMAD1/5/9 provides strong evidence that FST specifically antagonizes Activin signaling without disrupting BMP signaling in this context.

results.result: Activin A rescues the FST-mediated delay in hair cell differentiation in cochlear explants. Hair cell differentiation occurs significantly earlier in Activin A-treated wild type explants compared to untreated controls, while FST overexpression significantly delays differentiation. When Activin A treatment is combined with FST overexpression, the delay is almost completely abolished, with no significant differences compared to wild type untreated explants.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are strongly supported by experimental data from cochlear explant rescue experiments (Figures 4B-F). The ability of Activin A to rescue FST-mediated delays provides compelling evidence that FST antagonizes hair cell differentiation in an Activin A-dependent manner, though other Activin-type ligands may also be involved.

results.result: FST overexpression (induced at E11.5) causes ectopic inner hair cell formation and severe delays in cochlear differentiation/maturation. At E18.5, R26-FST cochlear tissue contains two rows of inner hair cells throughout the basal half (instead of one row), with correspondingly increased inner phalangeal cell density. The auditory sensory epithelium is 30% shorter than controls, hair cells have less mature stereocilia, and apical hair cells lack stereocilia completely.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 are well-supported by morphological analysis and quantitative measurements (Figures 5A-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The observation that inner phalangeal cell density also increases (C65) provides important evidence against a supporting cell-to-hair cell conversion mechanism. The multiple phenotypic abnormalities are consistent and statistically significant.

results.result: FST induction at E13.0 (one day later than E11.5) does not affect cochlear length but still causes ectopic inner hair cell formation and delayed hair cell maturation. The length of the auditory sensory epithelium at E17.5 is not significantly different from controls, but ectopic inner hair cells are observed (highest number in the basal portion), and hair cell stereocilia have a less mature phenotype compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 are supported by experimental measurements and morphological analysis (Figures 6A-B). The temporal specificity of the phenotype (affecting patterning and maturation but not length when induced later) provides important information about the critical windows for FST action, though sample size for length measurement is modest (n=3).

results.result: Conditional knockout of Inhba (Activin A) results in hair cell maturation and patterning defects similar to but milder than FST overexpression. Inhba cKO does not alter overall cochlear morphology or sensory epithelium length at P0, but shows a significant increase in ectopic inner hair cells (concentrated in the basal segment) and less mature hair cell stereocilia throughout the cochlea compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 are supported by experimental data from Inhba conditional knockout mice (Figures 6C-D). The milder phenotype compared to FST overexpression suggests FST may target additional Activin-type ligands beyond Activin A. However, the sample size for length measurement is small (n=2), which limits confidence in the statistical conclusion about unchanged length.

results.result: FST likely disrupts multiple Activin-related signaling mechanisms beyond Activin A in the developing cochlea. The milder defects in Inhba mutants compared to FST transgenic animals suggest additional targets. GDF11 is identified as the predominant Activin-type ligand in the developing cochlea based on RT-qPCR analysis, while Inhbb and Mstn are expressed at very low or undetectable levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 and C118 are supported by comparative phenotypic analysis and RT-qPCR expression data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The inference that FST targets additional ligands beyond Activin A is reasonable given the phenotypic differences, and GDF11 is a plausible candidate based on its high expression and known FST binding. However, functional validation of GDF11's role would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: FST overexpression delays pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal along the longitudinal cochlear axis but does not disrupt the apical-to-basal gradient. When EdU is administered at E13.5 and analyzed at E18.5, basal hair cells incorporate EdU at similar rates (~25%) in both control and FST overexpressing animals, but mid and apical hair cells in FST overexpressing cochleae show robust EdU incorporation while controls show little to none. Apical hair cells still incorporate EdU at lower rates than basal hair cells in FST tissue, indicating the gradient is preserved.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are well-supported by EdU incorporation data (Figures 7A-E). The preservation of the apical-to-basal gradient despite delayed cell cycle exit is an important observation that distinguishes effects on timing from effects on spatial patterning. The data clearly demonstrate region-specific effects of FST overexpression.

results.result: A medial-to-lateral gradient of terminal mitosis exists in wild type cochlear tissue, with inner hair cell progenitors withdrawing from the cell cycle prior to outer hair cell progenitors. In the mid-turn of control cochleae, more than 6% of outer hair cells are EdU-positive while no inner hair cells incorporate EdU. This distinct medial-to-lateral gradient is lost in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue, where inner and outer hair cells incorporate EdU at similar rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 and C128-C129 are supported by EdU incorporation data (Figures 7D-E, 8E-F) demonstrating a previously unrecognized radial gradient of cell cycle exit. This is a novel finding with important implications for understanding hair cell production. The loss of this gradient in FST overexpressing tissue provides mechanistic insight into the ectopic inner hair cell phenotype.

results.result: Prolonged EdU labeling (E14.5-E17.5) reveals that FST overexpression causes prolonged proliferation of inner hair cell progenitors. Supporting cells and hair cells in R26-FST animals incorporate EdU at much higher frequency than controls. In control tissue, outer hair cells (12.1%) incorporate EdU at significantly higher rates than inner hair cells (1.5%), but in FST tissue inner hair cells incorporate EdU at similar or higher rates than outer hair cells. In the apex of FST tissue, only inner hair cells and inner phalangeal cells are EdU-labeled.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are strongly supported by EdU incorporation data from prolonged labeling experiments (Figures 8A-F). The specific labeling of inner hair cells and inner phalangeal cells in the apex of FST tissue (C93) provides particularly compelling evidence that ectopic inner hair cells arise from prolonged proliferation rather than fate conversion. The inference in C94 is well-justified by the data.

results.result: At the peak of terminal mitosis (E13.5), Fst expression becomes restricted to the lateral portion of the pro-sensory domain, suggesting inner hair cell progenitors experience higher levels of Activin-type signaling than outer hair cell progenitors. This radial gradient of Activin signaling constitutes a novel mechanism for limiting the number of inner hair cells produced in the mammalian cochlea.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 1A) and the functional data demonstrating differential cell cycle exit timing. The inference in C131 about differential Activin-type signaling exposure is reasonable based on the expression patterns. The conclusion in C132 about a novel mechanism is justified by the combination of expression data and functional experiments, though the term 'novel' should be interpreted in the context of this specific system.

results.result: A local gradient of Activin A signaling within the auditory sensory epithelium times the longitudinal gradient of hair cell differentiation, and Activin-type signaling regulates a radial gradient of terminal mitosis that limits inner hair cell production. Activin A acts as a pro-differentiation signal, as demonstrated by exogenous Activin A triggering premature differentiation in explants and disruption of Activin A signaling (via FST overexpression or Inhba deletion) causing delayed differentiation in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, and C95 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript and are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence including expression analysis, gain-of-function (FST overexpression), loss-of-function (Inhba deletion), and rescue experiments. The combination of longitudinal and radial gradients provides a sophisticated model for how Activin signaling controls both timing and number of hair cells produced.

results.result: Activin signaling does not directly activate Atoh1 expression or interfere with SHH signaling, but rather acts indirectly through inhibition of Id3 and Id4 expression. Brief (4 hr) Activin A treatment does not significantly increase Atoh1 transcript, and neither over-activation nor loss of Activin signaling alters expression of SHH target genes (Hey1, Hey2, Fgf20). The authors propose a model where Wnt/β-catenin signaling initiates Atoh1 expression while Activin signaling enhances it along the longitudinal axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99, C101, and C103 are supported by experimental data showing no changes in SHH target genes and no immediate Atoh1 response to brief Activin treatment. The indirect mechanism through Id gene repression is well-supported. However, the proposed model in C103 integrating Wnt and Activin signaling is speculative and based on inference from the current data combined with prior literature rather than direct experimental validation in this study.

results.result: FST overexpression delays pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal and differentiation through mechanisms that may involve p27/Kip1 protein stability/activity and increased Id3/Id4 expression. The expression pattern of Fst mimics that of Lin28b (both highly expressed in pro-sensory cells and downregulated following a basal-to-apical gradient). No changes in p27/Kip1 mRNA are observed with FST overexpression, suggesting effects on protein level rather than transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by experimental data, but C112-C114 involve speculative mechanisms. The lack of p27/Kip1 mRNA changes (C112) is documented, but the inference about protein stability/activity (C113) and the contribution of increased Id3/Id4 (C114) are reasonable hypotheses that lack direct experimental validation. The comparison to Lin28b (C108-C109) is interesting but does not establish a functional connection.

results.result: FST overexpression and Inhba ablation result in overproduction of inner hair cells through prolonged progenitor proliferation rather than disruption of BMP signaling or fate conversion. FST overexpression does not disrupt or significantly reduce BMP signaling (unchanged P-SMAD1/5/9 levels and Id1-3 expression), and the increased inner phalangeal cell density argues against supporting cell-to-hair cell conversion.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 and C126-C127 are supported by experimental data showing ectopic inner hair cells, intact BMP signaling markers, and increased supporting cell density. The inference in C127 about prolonged proliferation is well-supported by the EdU incorporation data. The exclusion of alternative mechanisms (BMP disruption, fate conversion) strengthens the proposed mechanism.

results.result: The mammalian auditory sensory epithelium has a highly stereotyped cellular pattern with precise rows of hair cells (one row of inner and three rows of outer hair cells). Differentiation is precisely timed and follows opposing gradients: pro-sensory cells exit the cell cycle in an apical-to-basal gradient while hair cell differentiation occurs in a basal-to-apical gradient. A shallower medial-to-lateral gradient also exists, with inner hair cells differentiating before outer hair cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C6-C7, and C135-C136 represent established knowledge in the field supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by observations in this manuscript. These claims provide essential background context for understanding the experimental findings but are not novel contributions of this work.

results.result: Prior work has established that SHH signaling from spiral ganglion neurons represses hair cell differentiation through maintaining HEY1/HEY2 expression, which antagonizes ATOH1 function. ID proteins downstream of BMP signaling also maintain pro-sensory cells in an undifferentiated state by interfering with ATOH1. Wnt/β-catenin signaling is required for hair cell formation but its activity pattern does not parallel the differentiation gradient. Inhba is expressed in a basal-to-apical gradient in the differentiating cochlea.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C23 summarize established knowledge from prior studies (supported by citations) that provides the scientific context for the current work. These claims accurately represent the state of the field and identify the gap (lack of understanding about pro-differentiation signals) that this study addresses. They are not novel findings but essential background.

results.result: Activins belong to the TGF-β superfamily and control diverse biological processes. Canonical TGF-β signaling is transduced by R-SMADs that form complexes with SMAD4 to activate target genes. FST antagonizes Activin signaling by encircling the Inhibin β dimer and blocking receptor binding. In the developing spinal cord, Activins are required for Atoh1 induction in neuronal progenitors. Within the differentiating auditory sensory epithelium, Fst and Inhba are expressed in opposing gradients.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28, C35, C133-C134 represent established knowledge about Activin/TGF-β signaling mechanisms and FST function, supported by citations to previous studies. Claim C134 about opposing gradients in the cochlea is supported by prior work (Son et al., 2015) and confirmed by data in this manuscript. These provide essential mechanistic context but are not novel findings.

results.result: Prior work has established various aspects of signaling pathway regulation in cochlear development and other systems: BMP signaling regulates Id1-3 expression; failure to downregulate Id3 inhibits hair cell formation; Wnt/β-catenin is required for hair cell specification; early SHH signaling establishes regional identity; Notch signaling regulates Inhba expression; TGF-β pathways inhibit proliferation through CDK inhibitors; p27/Kip1 regulates pro-sensory cell cycle exit; ID proteins are associated with proliferative states; FST can be detected early in otocyst development; GDF11-FST axis regulates progenitor cells in other sensory tissues; Activin signaling has different effects in chicken versus mammalian auditory epithelia; FST can interfere with BMP signaling in some tissues; BMP signaling is critical for cochlear patterning.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C100, C102, C104-C106, C110-C111, C115-C116, C119-C121, C124-C125 represent established knowledge from prior studies (all supported by citations) that provides context for interpreting the current findings. These claims accurately represent relevant background information but are not novel contributions of this work.

results.result: Induction of FST overexpression at E11.5 or E14.5 results in neonatal lethality of R26-FST transgenic animals, limiting analysis to late embryonic stages.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is a straightforward observation about the experimental system that is important for understanding the limitations of the study. This is a technical constraint rather than a scientific finding, but it is clearly documented and affects the interpretation of results.

results.result: In the developing cortex, Activin signaling promotes interneuron differentiation through inhibition of SHH signaling.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is supported by a citation to previous work (Cambray et al., 2012) and is used as a comparison point to discuss potential mechanisms in the cochlea. This is background information from another system rather than a finding of the current study.
